  "title": "Kinematic-Decomposition-Guided Data Generation for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Bayesian Acquisition over Failure Structure",
  "core_problem": "Humanoid loco-manipulation policies trained via imitation learning exhibit compound failure modes arising from interactions between kinematic subsystems—balance, locomotion, manipulation, and whole-body coordination. Isaac Lab Mimic can procedurally generate thousands of G1 loco-manipulation demonstrations from a handful of teleoperated sources, but generates uniformly without knowledge of which scenarios cause downstream policy failures. When failures do occur, they are compositional: a dropped object during turning may result from a balance deficit (CoM shifted by payload), a locomotion instability (insufficient support polygon during turn), and a coordination failure (upper-body tracking conflicting with lower-body stability). Existing failure-guided data generation methods (IntervenGen, RESample, FailSafe, RACER) treat the robot as a monolithic agent—they identify failure states or coverage gaps but do not decompose failures along kinematic subsystems or use the decomposition to parameterize what scenarios to generate. How can we exploit the humanoid kinematic structure to decompose policy failures into subsystem contributions and use this decomposition to guide targeted procedural demonstration generation?",
  "opportunity": "Isaac Lab Mimic now provides native G1 loco-manipulation data generation: PR #3150 added the G1 pick-place loco-manipulation environment with 92% datagen success rate, and PR #3992 (merged Dec 2025) added loco-manipulation datagen APIs that treat the robot base as an end effector with navigation controller support. Isaac Lab 2.3 further integrates SkillGen with MimicGen for collision-free manipulation planning, and Isaac Lab Arena provides additional G1 loco-manipulation tasks (box-transport-to-bin). This infrastructure enables closed-loop experiments—generate data, train policy, evaluate, decompose failures, generate targeted data—entirely within a single GPU-accelerated framework. Meanwhile, Data Scaling Laws (arXiv:2410.18647, ICLR 2025) empirically demonstrate that diversity matters more than volume for robot imitation learning, directly motivating targeted over uniform generation. The gap: no method (1) decomposes whole-body humanoid failures into kinematic subsystem contributions using physics-based signals, (2) maps these decomposed failures to procedural generation parameters, and (3) learns this mapping via an acquisition function rather than fixed rules. IntervenGen generates corrective interventions at failure states but doesn't decompose why failures occur. RESample identifies coverage gaps but not kinematic failure modes. FailSafe and RACER generate failure-recovery pairs semantically but don't parameterize generation conditions via physics. HOTU decomposes humanoid structure for cross-embodiment skill transfer but not for failure-guided data targeting. OmniRetarget generates 8+ hours of G1 trajectories via retargeting but uniformly, without failure feedback. ALMI demonstrates that upper/lower body decomposition enables robust humanoid policies, but this structural insight has never been applied to data generation.",
  "landscape": "**Failure-guided data generation (manipulation).** IntervenGen (CoRL 2024, arXiv:2405.01472) autonomously generates corrective intervention datasets from ~10 human demonstrations, achieving 39x robustness improvement for single-arm manipulation in robosuite—but generates corrections AT failure states without decomposing failure causes or parameterizing generation conditions. RESample (ICRA 2026, arXiv:2510.17640) uses a coverage function to identify low-density regions in VLA training data and actively samples exploratory actions, achieving 12% improvement with 10-20% additional samples—but targets distribution coverage gaps rather than kinematic failure modes. FailSafe (arXiv:2510.01642) automatically produces diverse failure cases paired with recovery actions using LLaVa-OneVision-7B, achieving 22.6% VLA improvement on ManiSkill tasks—but uses semantic/VLM-based failure identification without physics-based decomposition. OmniRetarget (arXiv:2509.26633) generates 8+ hours of G1 whole-body loco-manipulation trajectories via interaction-mesh-based retargeting—uniform distribution, not failure-guided. DexMimicGen (ICRA 2025) generates 21K demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation but operates in robosuite/MuJoCo with GR-1 upper body only (locked lower body), and generates uniformly. SoftMimicGen (arXiv:2603.25725) extends to deformable objects—still uniform. **Humanoid decomposition for learning.** HOTU (IEEE RAM 2025, arXiv:2412.15166) decomposes humanoid structures into functional components trained independently and dynamically coordinated for cross-embodiment skill transfer—decomposition for transfer, not for failure analysis or data targeting. ALMI (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2504.14305) uses adversarial upper/lower body decoupled training for robust humanoid policies—demonstrates the kinematic decomposition principle for control, not for data generation. **Failure analysis without generation.** Unsupervised Failure Taxonomies (arXiv:2506.06570) discovers failure modes from deployment logs via VLM clustering—does not close the loop to generation, not physics-based. RoboFail (Dec 2024) analyzes failures without generating corrective data. **Self-improving data flywheels.** DexFlyWheel (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2509.23829) implements a self-improving flywheel via IL + residual RL + rollout augmentation for dexterous hands—treats robot as monolithic system without kinematic decomposition. SILVR (ICLR 2026, arXiv:2506.06658) achieves iterative video-model self-improvement on single-arm MetaWorld tasks—not humanoid, uses expensive video generation. Hi-WM (arXiv:2604.21741) enables failure-targeted corrections via world models but requires human-in-the-loop and only handles dual-arm manipulation.",
  "approach": "We propose a closed-loop data generation pipeline for G1 humanoid loco-manipulation that decomposes policy failures along kinematic subsystems and uses learned Bayesian acquisition over the decomposition space to target Isaac Lab Mimic's procedural generation. The system runs for 2 iterative cycles across 3 tasks entirely within Isaac Lab.\n\n**1. Kinematic-Structure-Aware Failure Decomposition.** After policy rollout across loco-manipulation scenarios, we collect failure episodes and extract a kinematic decomposition vector from physics signals available in Isaac Lab's simulation state: (a) Balance—center-of-mass deviation from support polygon centroid, angular momentum magnitude, ZMP margin violations; (b) Locomotion—foot placement error relative to planned contacts, ground reaction force asymmetry, gait phase deviation; (c) Manipulation—end-effector tracking error, grasp force adequacy, object pose drift; (d) Coordination—normalized cross-correlation between upper-body joint torques and lower-body stability metrics (CoM acceleration, ZMP rate of change), quantifying mutual interference. Each dimension is normalized against task-specific baselines computed from successful demonstrations, yielding a vector in [0,1]^4 characterizing the failure profile. We cluster failures in this decomposed space using HDBSCAN, yielding interpretable clusters like 'balance-dominant failures during heavy-object transport' or 'coordination-dominant failures during reach-while-walking.'\n\n**2. Bayesian Acquisition over Decomposition-Parameterized Generation Space.** Each failure cluster maps to Isaac Lab Mimic generation parameters. In the first cycle, we use physics-informed rules as a warm start: balance-dominant clusters → increase object mass range, narrow navigation corridor, add slope to terrain; locomotion-dominant clusters → increase terrain roughness, step height variation, tighter turns; manipulation-dominant clusters → vary object geometry, increase reach distance, add pose constraints; coordination-dominant clusters → compose challenging locomotion with simultaneous manipulation demands, vary timing offsets between locomotion and manipulation phases. After the first cycle, we fit a Gaussian Process over the observed mapping from (decomposition-vector region, generation parameter settings) → measured policy improvement (success rate delta on held-out evaluation scenarios). A UCB acquisition function then selects the generation parameters for cycle 2, balancing exploitation of known-effective generation strategies with exploration of under-sampled decomposition regions. This converts the system from rule-based engineering into Bayesian optimization over the kinematic-decomposition-parameterized generation space, and produces an empirical answer to: which kinematic failure modes benefit most from targeted data generation?\n\n**3. Targeted Generation via Isaac Lab Mimic.** We use Isaac Lab Mimic's DataGenerator API with the body end-effector and navigation controller support (PR #3992) to generate demonstrations targeting identified failure conditions. Source demonstrations are selected via NearestNeighborObject or NearestNeighborRobotDistance strategies, adapted to the targeted scene parameters (modified terrain, object properties, navigation waypoints), and verified for physical feasibility via Isaac Lab's GPU-accelerated physics. This generates 1000-2000 targeted demonstrations per cycle (~20-40 minutes on RTX hardware, CPU+GPU physics, negligible compared to policy training).\n\n**Evaluation.** 3 G1 loco-manipulation tasks: (1) Isaac-PickPlace-Locomanipulation-G1-Abs-v0 (existing Isaac Lab environment, pick object from table, navigate to target, place), (2) G1 box-transport-to-bin (existing Isaac Lab Arena task, navigate/pick/transport box to bin), (3) carry-and-navigate with terrain variation (minor extension of task 1 with extended navigation segments over randomized terrain patches and heavier objects). These tasks already exist or require minimal modification (task 3: terrain randomization + extended navigation waypoints in existing env config). Baselines: (a) uniform Isaac Lab Mimic generation (same total demo budget, no failure targeting), (b) aggregate failure targeting (failure signal without kinematic decomposition—treats robot as monolithic), (c) rules-only mapping (no GP acquisition, warm-start rules throughout), (d) random augmentation baseline. Primary metrics: task success rate, data efficiency (success rate improvement per generated demonstration), per-subsystem failure rate reduction. 2 iterative cycles × 3 tasks × 4 conditions = 24 policy training runs total.\n\n**Limitations acknowledged.** (1) GP with UCB may have limited benefit with only 2 cycles of data (k=4 decomposition dimensions, ~8-12 generation parameter configurations per cycle); the rules-only ablation quantifies this. (2) Physics-based decomposition requires simulator state access, limiting direct transfer of the decomposition module to real deployment (though the generated data and resulting policies transfer via standard sim-to-real). (3) Validation is limited to G1 in Isaac Lab simulation with 3 tasks; generalization to other embodiments (e.g., H1, Atlas) requires re-calibrating decomposition baselines. (4) Cross-correlation-based coordination metrics may conflate intentional upper/lower body coupling with pathological interference; we add a causality check using Granger causality on joint torque time series to distinguish.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MISSING WORK — Fail2Progress (CoRL 2025, arXiv:2509.01746): Failure-guided targeted data generation using Stein variational inference. Different level of abstraction (symbolic/relational vs. physics-based) and different embodiment (mobile manipulator vs. humanoid), but shares the core motivation of 'learn from failures to generate targeted sim data.' Must cite and differentiate: Fail2Progress operates on symbolic relational mismatches for task-level skill effect models, while this proposal uses dynamics-level physics signals for low-level policy improvement.", "MISSING WORK — BayRn (RA-L 2021, arXiv:2003.02471): Uses Bayesian optimization over domain randomization distribution parameters for sim-to-real transfer. Directly precedents the GP+UCB-over-environment-parameters component. Must cite to contextualize the BO contribution.", "MISSING WORK — BO-Terrain Curriculum for Quadrupeds (Systems Science & Control Engineering, 2025): Uses Bayesian optimization to predict and select optimal training terrains for quadrupedal robots. The closest methodological prior art for the GP+UCB terrain/scenario selection component. Must cite and differentiate: they parameterize by terrain geometry, you parameterize by kinematic failure decomposition.", "MISSING WORK — SA2RT (arXiv:2507.08303, 2025): Selective adversarial training for humanoid G1 that identifies policy vulnerabilities and generates targeted perturbations, improving terrain traversal by 40%. Directly relevant as an alternative approach to targeted robustness improvement for the same robot (G1). Must cite; could serve as an additional baseline or at minimum related work.", "MISSING WORK — RoboGate (arXiv:2603.22126, 2026): Uses two-stage boundary-focused sampling across 8D parameter space to map failure boundaries in simulation with 40K+ experiments. Related to systematic failure characterization in parameterized environments, though focuses on deployment safety rather than data generation.", "VENUE ERROR: IntervenGen was published at IROS 2024 (IEEE IROS, DOI:10.1109/IROS58592.2024.10801523), NOT CoRL 2024. Fix citation.", "VENUE ERROR: RESample was submitted to IROS 2026, NOT ICRA 2026. Fix citation.", "TASK NAME ERROR: Isaac Lab Arena's G1 loco-manipulation task is registered as 'g1_locomanip_pnp' (pick-and-place), not 'box-transport-to-bin'. The task semantics are similar (G1 navigates, picks box, places in bin) but the exact name 'box-transport-to-bin' does not appear in the codebase.", "GP+UCB CONTRIBUTION RISK: With only 2 cycles × 3 tasks producing ~24 observations in a 4D decomposition + multi-dimensional generation parameter space, the GP posterior will be extremely uncertain. The rules-only ablation correctly quantifies this, but if GP shows no improvement, the paper's contribution framing needs to gracefully degrade. Currently, the GP acquisition is positioned as a co-equal contribution alongside the decomposition—it should be reframed as a secondary enhancement with the decomposition framework as the primary contribution.", "MISSING CURRICULUM LEARNING CONTEXT: The proposal's core loop—evaluate policy, identify weaknesses, generate targeted training data—is functionally equivalent to automatic curriculum generation. The paper should cite and differentiate from ACCEL (ICML 2022), Active Domain Randomization (CoRL 2020), and the broader UED literature. The key differentiator is kinematic decomposition providing a structured, interpretable parameterization versus generic regret/coverage-based methods."]
Feedback: The core insight—kinematic decomposition of humanoid failures to parameterize targeted data generation—is genuinely novel and well-matched to Isaac Lab Mimic's infrastructure. The proposal has improved substantially from Rounds 1-2. To reach pass threshold:

1. **CITE MISSING RELATED WORK (Critical for CoRL reviewers)**: Add Fail2Progress (CoRL 2025), BayRn (RA-L 2021), BO-Terrain Curriculum for Quadrupeds (2025), SA2RT (arXiv 2025), RoboGate (arXiv 2026), Active Domain Randomization (CoRL 2020), and ACCEL (ICML 2022). For each, provide explicit differentiation. The key argument: prior failure-guided methods (Fail2Progress, IntervenGen, RESample) treat the robot as monolithic and use symbolic/semantic failure signals; prior BO-curriculum methods (BayRn, BO-Terrain) parameterize by environment geometry without failure-driven decomposition; this work uniquely bridges physics-based kinematic failure analysis with BO-guided procedural generation.

2. **FIX CITATION ERRORS**: IntervenGen → IROS 2024; RESample → submitted IROS 2026; Arena task → g1_locomanip_pnp.

3. **REFRAME CONTRIBUTION HIERARCHY**: Make the kinematic decomposition framework the primary contribution (novel, interpretable, humanoid-specific). Position GP+UCB as a secondary contribution that converts the pipeline from engineering to optimization. Explicitly state: 'Even if the GP acquisition does not outperform physics-informed rules with 2 cycles of data, the decomposition framework itself provides the first systematic method for diagnosing and targeting kinematic failure modes in humanoid data generation.'

4. **CONSIDER 3 CYCLES**: Your compute budget allows it (~100 H100-hours used of 160 budget based on verified training times). 3 cycles would give the GP ~36 observations and make the BO contribution more credible. Even if timeline is tight, cycle 3 can run the GP-selected condition only (not full ablation), adding ~10 H100-hours.

5. **ADD SA2RT AS RELATED COMPARISON**: SA2RT targets G1 robustness via adversarial training. While not a direct baseline (it uses adversarial perturbation, not data generation), discussing why targeted data generation complements adversarial training would strengthen the positioning.

6. **STRENGTHEN IMPACT CLAIM**: Cite AGILE (arXiv 2026) and Embedding Classical Balance Control (arXiv 2026) to show that the physics signals you use (CoM, ZMP, centroidal momentum) are already validated as meaningful for humanoid RL—your novelty is using them post-hoc for failure diagnosis and data targeting rather than as online training signals.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

## 针对 Review 意见的定向搜索

对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，执行以下搜索流程：

1. **如果 reviewer 说'已有类似工作'**：
   - 搜索 reviewer 提到的论文，用 WebFetch 实际阅读
   - 搜索该论文的 cited-by，找到后续跟进工作
   - 明确你的 idea 与这些工作的差异化点——如果差异化不够，必须 pivot

2. **如果 reviewer 说'SOTA 过时'**：
   - 用 Papers With Code 查看当前排行榜
   - 搜索过去 6 个月的最新方法
   - 更新你的 landscape 和 baseline

3. **如果 reviewer 说'可行性有问题'**：
   - 搜索类似规模实验的实际成本和时间线
   - 搜索 GitHub 上是否有可复用的实现
   - 搜索相关数据集/模型的可获取性

4. **如果 reviewer 说'novelty 不足'**：
   - 对核心方法尽量做 3-5 种不同关键词组合的搜索
   - 搜索相邻领域是否有类似思路
   - 如果确实 novelty 不足，考虑 major revision 或 pivot

- Use WebSearch to find updated information if the reviewer flagged outdated claims.
- You have full freedom in how much to change:
  - Minor fix: if only specific details are wrong, correct them and keep everything else.
  - Major revision: if the approach is fundamentally flawed but the core problem is valid, you may redesign the approach entirely.
  - Pivot: if the reviewer's feedback reveals that the core problem itself is invalid (e.g., the gap no longer exists), you may propose a RELATED but substantially different idea that builds on the same research area. This is preferred over forcing a doomed idea to pass review.
- The output replaces the original idea (same tracking ID). Whether you make a small tweak or a full pivot, output a COMPLETE JSON object with ALL fields filled.
- In the output JSON, include a "change_type" field with one of: "minor", "major", or "pivot" to indicate the scope of your changes.
- Output the revised idea as a COMPLETE JSON object (same schema as original, plus "change_type").

- **arXiv:** 2003.02471 (submitted March 2020, last revised January 2021)

### Core Problem and Motivation

Standard domain randomization samples physics parameters (masses, frictions, motor constants) from a fixed, hand-specified distribution during training. This is suboptimal because those distributions are not chosen to maximize real-world policy performance — they are set from engineering intuition alone. BayRn reframes the choice of that distribution as an optimization problem.

### How Bayesian Optimization Is Used Over Domain Randomization Parameters

BayRn treats the domain randomization distribution parameters themselves — e.g., the mean and standard deviation of a body mass, friction coefficient, or actuator gain — as the decision variables for a Bayesian optimization loop. The outer loop is:

1. **Propose** a candidate domain parameter distribution (the "source domain") using a GP-based acquisition function.
2. **Train** a policy in simulation using that distribution.
3. **Evaluate** the trained policy on the real robot (or a held-out target simulation) to get a sparse scalar return signal.
4. **Update** the GP surrogate model with the (distribution parameters → real-world return) observation.
5. Repeat until budget exhausted; deploy the best policy found.

This makes BayRn a "black-box sim-to-real algorithm": the inner RL training is treated as opaque, and BO navigates the outer space of distribution hyperparameters. The acquisition function used is **Expected Improvement (EI)**, with a zero-mean GP prior using a **Matérn 5/2 kernel**, implemented via the BoTorch library with normalized inputs and standardized outputs. (The paper explicitly uses EI, not UCB — a key clarification relative to the "GP+UCB" framing sometimes used to describe similar methods.)

1. **Quanser Furuta Pendulum** — an underactuated swing-up and balance task. Domain parameters randomized include pendulum link masses, inertias, and motor constants.
2. **Barrett WAM Robotic Arm** — a ball-in-a-cup task where the robot must swing a ball on a string into a cup. Domain parameters include arm link masses, joint friction, and motor gains.

Experiments were run in both sim-to-sim (surrogate "real" environment) and true sim-to-real settings. 20 policies were trained per algorithm (varying random seeds), each evaluated 5 times, for 700 total rollouts.

### Baselines

Three baselines were compared:
1. Fixed/uniform domain randomization (non-adaptive, hand-specified distributions)
2. A manual parameter-tuning approach
3. An alternative adaptation method (exact name varies across versions but likely includes a system identification or prior-informed approach)

BayRn demonstrated significantly improved sim-to-real transfer compared to fixed DR baselines while substantially reducing the required prior knowledge about the domain parameter uncertainty. The key contribution is data efficiency: BO finds good distribution parameters with very few real-world evaluations (a scarce and expensive resource on physical robots).

BayRn is closely related to the GP+UCB paradigm but makes two specific choices: it uses **EI rather than UCB** as the acquisition function, and the input space is the **parameters of the randomization distribution** (e.g., mean/std of each physics parameter), not the physics parameters themselves directly. Uses GP+EI over domain randomization distribution parameters for sim-to-real transfer. We optimize generation parameters guided by kinematic failure decomposition—the input space is (failure-decomposition region × generation parameters) and the objective is policy improvement on identified failure modes.
